seoul-gu/강서구: Seoul's western gateway, home to Gimpo Airport. The new Magok district has risen here.
seoul-gu/양천구: Mok-dong New Town and a street of broadcasters. Split off from Gangseo-gu in 1988.
seoul-gu/구로구: Where the Guro Industrial Complex became the G-Valley digital complex. One of Seoul's highest shares of foreign residents.
seoul-gu/금천구: Split off from Guro-gu in 1995. Gasan Digital Complex and Siheung-daero run through it.
seoul-gu/영등포구: Yeouido and the National Assembly. The site of Korea's first modern industrial zone.
seoul-gu/마포구: Hongdae and Sangam. In the Joseon era, Mapo Ferry was where goods from the Yellow Sea entered Seoul.
seoul-gu/서대문구: Seodaemun Prison and Independence Gate. Yonsei and Ewha Womans universities sit side by side.
seoul-gu/은평구: The western gateway to Bukhansan. Home to Jingwansa Temple and Eunpyeong Hanok Village.
seoul-gu/종로구: The heart of the Joseon dynasty for five hundred years. Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung both stand here.
seoul-gu/중구: Myeong-dong and Namdaemun Market. The fewest residents in Seoul, and the most people passing through.
seoul-gu/용산구: Itaewon and Hannam-dong. Yongsan Park is taking shape where the US military base left.
seoul-gu/동작구: Seoul National Cemetery and Noryangjin. The oldest ferry crossing south of the Han River was here.
seoul-gu/관악구: Gwanaksan and Seoul National University. Around Sillim-dong, the share of single-person households is among the highest in the country.
seoul-gu/서초구: The Supreme Court and Seoul Arts Center. Seoul's southern axis, taking in Banpo and Yangjaecheon.
seoul-gu/강남구: Split off from Seongdong-gu in 1975. The farmland of Yeongdong became a city centre in 50 years.
seoul-gu/송파구: Site of Wiryeseong, Baekje's first capital. Home to Seokchon Lake and Olympic Park.
seoul-gu/강동구: Seoul's easternmost district. The Amsa-dong Prehistoric Site preserves a village from 6,000 years ago.
seoul-gu/광진구: Konkuk University Entrance and Achasan. Seoul Children's Grand Park has stood here since 1973.
seoul-gu/성동구: Where Seongsu-dong's handmade-shoe street turned into a café street. Home to Seoul Forest.
seoul-gu/동대문구: Dongdaemun, the gate it is named after, actually stands in Jongno-gu. Home to Gyeongdong Market and Hongneung.
seoul-gu/중랑구: Split off from Dongdaemun-gu in 1988. Each spring the Jungnangcheon rose tunnel opens.
seoul-gu/노원구: Planned in the 1980s as large apartment estates. Seoul's densest belt of hagwon (private academies).
seoul-gu/도봉구: Seoul's northernmost district. Dobongsan is both its name and its border.
seoul-gu/강북구: At the foot of Bukhansan. Home to the April 19th National Cemetery and Suyu-ri.
seoul-gu/성북구: The name means north of the city wall. Home to Seongbuk-dong's writers' village and embassy street.
gangseo-dong/공항동: A dong that holds the whole of Gimpo International Airport. The largest in Gangseo-gu, twice the size of the second largest.
gangseo-dong/방화2동: Banghwa (傍花) means 'beside the flowers', from the flowers that once covered Gaehwasan. The northernmost part of Gangseo-gu.
gangseo-dong/방화3동: The northwestern edge wedged between the Han River and Gaehwasan. The district boundary runs at a slant along the river.
gangseo-dong/방화1동: The southernmost of the three Banghwa dongs. It sits on the route linking the airport side and the Hwagok side.
gangseo-dong/가양1동: Stretched along the Han River, the second-largest dong in Gangseo-gu. Gayang (加陽) takes one character from each of two old village names.
gangseo-dong/가양2동: The middle of the three Gayang dongs. It forms a narrow strip between the Han River and Deungchon-dong.
gangseo-dong/가양3동: The Gayang dong hugging the bank of the Han River. Across the river lie Mapo and Sangam.
gangseo-dong/염창동: Yeomchang (鹽倉) means salt warehouse. Salt shipped up from the Yellow Sea was stored here and sent on to the capital. The eastern tip of Gangseo-gu.
gangseo-dong/등촌1동: Deungchon (登村) means a village perched up on a ridge. The smallest of the three Deungchon dongs.
gangseo-dong/등촌3동: The westernmost of the three Deungchon dongs. Wedged between Gayang-dong and Hwagok-dong, it runs long from north to south.
gangseo-dong/발산1동: Balsan (鉢山) comes from a hill shaped like an upturned baru, a monk's alms bowl. The fourth-largest dong in Gangseo-gu.
gangseo-dong/화곡3동: Hwagok (禾谷) means 'rice valley': land where rice grew well. One of the smallest of the seven Hwagok dongs.
gangseo-dong/우장산동: Ujangsan (雨裝山) was the hill for rain rituals. It got its name because people climbed it dressed ready for rain.
gangseo-dong/화곡1동: The southern edge of Gangseo-gu. Go further south and you are in Yangcheon-gu.
gangseo-dong/화곡8동: The numbers skip — 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 — because dongs 5 and 7 were merged into other dongs.
gangseo-dong/화곡2동: The smallest of Gangseo-gu's twenty dongs, and the southernmost.
gangseo-dong/화곡4동: The eastern end of the seven Hwagok dongs. It stands shoulder to shoulder with Deungchon 2-dong.
gangseo-dong/등촌2동: The easternmost of the three Deungchon dongs. It splits Hwagok-dong and Yeomchang-dong with a north–south line.
gangseo-dong/화곡6동: A dong set between Hwagokbon-dong and Deungchon-dong. It takes in the eastern slope of Ujangsan.
gangseo-dong/화곡본동: The original dong left after the other Hwagok dongs split off. It borders seven dongs, the most neighbours in Gangseo-gu.
